speaker_role: current admissions officers (Northeastern University director of global enrollment strategies; UVA associate dean of admission; Notre Dame director of international admissions) plus two independent college counselors (Guidewell/ESM Prep), moderated by Summit Educational Group
commercial_incentive: Yes - moderated/hosted by Summit Educational Group and ESM Prep/Guidewell, which are test-prep and counseling businesses, though the panelists' institutional comments are not sales pitches
key_insights: Northeastern's rep states they do not look at AP exam scores at all in the admissions review process, only the coursework/rigor; a 4 or 5 only matters later for college credit after enrollment

All panelists agree students from 'non-AP' schools are not disadvantaged - school profiles and school reports communicate curriculum rigor, and admissions officers evaluate rigor 'in context' of what a school actually offers
UVA's rep says a course not taken because the school doesn't offer it (e.g., no AP Calc) will not be penalized if the school profile confirms it isn't available

Panelists across all three schools say self-reported AP scores that are simply not submitted are not assumed to be bad - they only evaluate the information actually provided, similar to test-optional SAT/ACT policies

General guidance is not to self-study and sit an AP exam for a course a student never took, since panelists say that hour is better spent on authentic, meaningful activities and self-studying doesn't replicate a full rigorous course
Core-subject APs (math, science, history, English, foreign language) are generally weighted more heavily for 'rigor' than electives like AP Personal Finance, per Northeastern's rep
Prospective engineering/pre-med applicants are expected to show subject alignment (e.g., calculus, physics for engineering) since a total absence raises unanswered questions, per counselor panelists
UVA's rep notes most of their students enter undecided and the school values curricular breadth so students can pivot majors after enrolling
Panelists say overloading on APs without matching activity depth is a common mistake; a 'B' or occasional lower AP score doesn't meaningfully hurt an otherwise strong application
Some colleges (not these panelists' specific practice necessarily) unweight GPA during review, recalculating it regardless of how the high school weights AP/honors courses
specific_numbers_or_facts: Northeastern receives over 100,000 applications per year (stated by Northeastern's director)
Northeastern only counts AP exam scores of 4 or 5 toward college credit; some schools also accept a 3 (per Northeastern's rep)
Notre Dame and UVA both indicated 4s/5s typically earn some form of college credit
notable_or_distinctive: A rare direct, named-institution confirmation that at least one major university (Northeastern) explicitly does not factor AP exam scores into the admissions decision at all, only the coursework itself - a specific, citable policy distinction between AP course rigor and AP test performance.
reliability_notes: This is a live webinar Q&A with real, named admissions officers from three specific universities, which raises reliability, but their statements reflect only their own institutions' current policies (as of the panel's recording) and shouldn't be generalized to all colleges; hosted/moderated by paid counseling and test-prep companies with a promotional framing around the event itself.
